section_1.title: Prerequisite: Defining the Planar Graph
section_1.content: Define a planar graph as a graph that can be drawn in a 2D plane without edges crossing. Introduce the concept of 'Faces' (the enclosed regions including the infinite outer region).
section_1.example: Visualizing a 'Spider-Man' web: If he shoots webs that don't cross, it's a planar graph. If they tangle, it's not.

section_2.title: Euler’s Characteristic Formula
section_2.content: Introduce the fundamental theorem: V - E + F = 2 (Vertices - Edges + Faces = 2). Explain that this relationship holds true for any connected planar graph.
section_2.example: An animation of a simple triangle (V=3, E=3, F=2) transforming into a square (V=4, E=4, F=2) to show the constant result of 2.

section_3.title: The Concept of Duality
section_3.content: Explain how to construct a dual graph: Place a dot (vertex) in every face of the original graph, and connect these dots if the faces share an edge.
section_3.example: Transforming a 'Cube' skeleton: Representing the 6 faces of a cube as 6 vertices in an octahedron-like dual structure.

section_4.title: The Duality Relationship
section_4.content: Show how the properties of the dual graph relate to the original: The number of vertices in the dual equals the number of faces in the original (V* = F, E* = E, F* = V).
section_4.example: A side-by-side animation of a map (regions) turning into a network of communication towers placed in the center of those regions.

section_5.title: Real-world Application & Summary
section_5.content: Summarize how these tools allow engineers to optimize circuit board layouts and map coloring problems. Recap: Planar graphs simplify complex systems into solvable geometry.
section_5.example: Designing a microchip: Showing how to reroute a 'crossing' wire by using duality to find an empty 'face' to pass through, ensuring no electrical short-circuits occur.
